Adult Whitson grenadiers (Macrourus whitsoni) attain a maximum recorded total length of 84 centimeters [Li = 84 centimeters], a size that places them among the larger-bodied members of the Macrourinae. The onset of reproductive activity is marked by a total length at puberty of 46 centimeters [Lp = 46 centimeters], a threshold that indicates a substantial period of somatic growth precedes the initiation of gametogenesis in this deep-sea species. Corresponding to these length metrics, the ultimate wet weight, or asymptotic adult mass, has been estimated at 3000 grams [Wwi = 3000 grams], while individuals at the pubertal stage achieve a wet weight at puberty of approximately 435 grams [Wwp = approximately 435 grams]. These weight estimates, derived from length-weight relationships calibrated on specimens of this species, reflect a life history strategy in which considerable mass accumulation occurs before the first allocation of resources to reproductive tissues, a pattern observed in other species of Macrourus that inhabit similar bathyal environments.

Reproductive output in Macrourus whitsoni has been characterized under controlled thermal conditions typical of its Antarctic habitat. At a stable water temperature of 2.5 °C [T = 2.5 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is expressed through a combination of fecundity and spawning frequency. Based on comparisons with the congener Macrourus carinatus, females of Whitson grenadier are estimated to produce roughly one clutch annually, with each spawning event containing approximately 101 eggs per event [N_R_i = approximately 101 eggs per event] and a frequency of one clutch annually [F_R_i = one clutch annually]. This total yearly output, when integrated over the reproductive lifespan, suggests a relatively low fecundity for a benthic teleost of this size. The reproductive schedule at this temperature likely represents an adaptation to the slow metabolic and growth rates imposed by the persistently cold waters of the Southern Ocean, where energetic constraints limit the number of oocytes that can be provisioned per season.

Life-history traits in Macrourus whitsoni also include a relatively extended lifespan, with the maximum documented longevity reaching 30 years [am = 30 years] at a mean ambient temperature of 4.5 °C [T = 4.5 °C]. This lifespan is consistent with the slow-paced demography characteristic of deep-sea macrourids, where low natural mortality rates and delayed maturity are common. The birth mass of this species is quite minute; a newly hatched larva, emerging from an egg of approximately 2.6 millimeters in diameter, possesses an estimated wet weight at birth of only 0.0092 grams [Wwb = 0.0092 grams]. This extremely small neonatal mass places the developing larva squarely within the planktonic size spectrum, relying upon a transient yolk reserve before the onset of exogenous feeding. The protracted 30-year lifespan (30 years) [am = 30 years] and the negligible hatchling mass together underscore a life-history strategy in which high early mortality is offset by iteroparous reproduction over many decades, a common pattern among long-lived, slow-growing deep-sea fishes at a temperature of 4.5 °C [T = 4.5 °C].

The reproductive biology of Macrourus whitsoni is further contextualized by its growth parameters, which link length to mass through allometric scaling. For example, the average adult asymptotic wet weight of 3000 grams [Wwi = 3000 grams] is attained only after decades of incremental growth in the cold waters of the Antarctic continental slope. In contrast, the mass at puberty, 435 grams [Wwp = 435 grams], is reached considerably earlier, when individuals have attained approximately half their ultimate length. These mass milestones, derived from length-weight relationships (using a coefficient of 0.00200 and an exponent of 3.21), reflect a pattern common among fish in stable, resource-limited environments: slow initial growth followed by a prolonged adult phase. The wet weight at puberty of 435 grams [Wwp = 435 grams] is roughly fifteen percent of the ultimate mass, a proportion that aligns with values observed in other deep-sea macrourids and that suggests the onset of reproductive allocation occurs only after a large fraction of somatic size has been achieved.

Finally, the early life stages of Macrourus whitsoni are characterized by the transition from a small, defenseless propagule to a feeding juvenile. The hatchling emerges at a wet weight of 0.0092 grams [Wwb = 0.0092 grams], a value based on a spherical egg diameter of 2.6 millimeters, comparable to that of Coryphaenoides rupestris. This minute mass necessitates a rapid transition to planktivory, as the endogenous yolk reserves are quickly exhausted. At a temperature of 2.5 °C [T = 2.5 °C], the same thermal regime under which the maximum annual reproduction rate of 101 eggs per year is achieved, larval growth is slow but steady, reflecting the energetic constraints of the cold environment. The ultimate total length of 84 centimeters [Li = 84 centimeters] and the immense lifespan of 30 years [am = 30 years] at 4.5 °C [T = 4.5 °C] together define a species that prioritizes longevity and low annual reproductive investment over rapid generation turnover, a classic bet-hedging strategy for life in the deep sea.
